data_schema.title: USDA Directive Extraction Schema v2.1 (DR/DM)
data_schema.description: Extracts metadata and structured policy statements from 3000 series USDA Departmental Regulation (DR) or Departmental Manual (DM). Governing rules: (1) Any field described as verbatim must be copied character-for-character from the source document. Never paraphrase, merge, abbreviate, summarize, or insert ellipses. (2) Do not infer. If the source does not support an optional field, leave the field out entirely. Never return an empty string or a guess. (3) Only the label fields in policy_statements (statement_kind, statement_function, modal_use, normative_force, actor_basis) are interpretations. Every other field is quoted or copied from the document.

document_type.description: Type of document as printed in the header, such as 'Departmental Regulation' or 'Departmental Manual'.

issuing_organization.description: Organization issuing the document, verbatim from the header.

issuing_location.description: Location of the issuing organization, verbatim from the header.

regulation_number.description: Official document number from the header, verbatim, for example 'DR 3105-001'.

subject.description: Subject or title of the document, verbatim from the header.

issue_date.description: Issue date from the header, as written.

expiration_date.description: Expiration date from the header, as written. Leave out if none is printed.

opi.description: Office of Primary Interest (OPI) from the header, verbatim.

supersedes.description: The prior document this document supersedes. Take all values from the supersession paragraph in the body (usually under Special Instructions/Cancellations), NOT from the header. Leave the whole object out if the document supersedes nothing.

document_number.description: Number of the superseded document as written in the supersession paragraph. If it is identical to this document's own number, still copy it from the supersession paragraph, not the header.

document_title.description: Title of the superseded document as written in the supersession paragraph.

document_date.description: Date of the superseded document as written in the supersession paragraph.

scope.description: The text of the Scope section, verbatim. Do not add words. Leave out if the document has no Scope section.

purpose.description: The text of the Purpose section, verbatim. Do not add words. Leave out if the document has no Purpose section.

inquiries.description: Contact information from the Inquiries section. Leave out any property the document does not state; never return an empty string.

office.description: Office or division named for inquiries, verbatim. Leave out if the document names no office.

email.description: Email address given for inquiries, verbatim, without trailing punctuation. Leave out if none is given.

table_of_contents.description: Top-level entries of the printed table of contents, in order, including appendices. Return an empty list if the document prints no table of contents.

section_number.description: Section or appendix identifier as printed, for example '1.' or 'Appendix A'.

section_title.description: Section or appendix title as printed in the table of contents.

page.description: Page number exactly as printed in the table of contents, for example '2' or 'A-1'. Copy it even if the section actually starts on a different page. Leave out if no page number is printed.

actors.description: Registry of every distinct entity that the policy text names in an acting role. One entry per entity. Include every entity used as actor_name in policy_statements. Also include entities the document names in a role without being directed to act (mark those mentioned_only). Documents (bylaws, regulations, directives) are NEVER actors and must not appear here. Return an empty list if the document names no actors.

name.description: The entity's name exactly as written in the policy text, without a leading article ('the') and without a possessive. Keep a compound name intact if the document writes it as one phrase, for example 'USDA Mission Areas, agencies, and staff offices'. This is the join key used by actor_name in policy_statements, so spell it identically there.

components.description: ONLY for a name that joins separate entities with commas or 'and' (for example 'USDA Mission Areas, agencies, and staff offices' gives 'USDA Mission Areas', 'agencies', 'staff offices'). NEVER split a job title from the organization that qualifies it ('Director of IT, Office of the Inspector General' is ONE position), and never split an organization name from the position it modifies ('Office of the Chief Information Officer (OCIO) Associate CIOs (ACIO)' is ONE group). Each component is a verbatim substring of the name. Leave out for single entities.

items.description: One verbatim component of a compound actor name.

actor_type.description: Kind of entity. Use exactly one of: position (a job title, singular or plural, for example 'USDA CIO' or 'Mission Area Assistant CIOs'), office (an organizational unit, for example 'OCIO Executive Secretariat'), council_or_body (a council, committee, board, or similar body), group (a category of organizations or units, not job titles, for example 'USDA Mission Areas, agencies, and staff offices'), external_entity (an entity outside the document's authority), program_or_system (an IT initiative, system, program, or project that the document says must act or conform).

binding_status.description: bound_by_this_document: the document directs, permits, or assigns a function or role to this entity and has authority over it. mentioned_only: the document names the entity but cannot or does not impose anything on it (for example a council or agency outside USDA that the document says a USDA body partners with).

policy_statements.description: Structured statements from the numbered body sections only (not the table of contents, not the appendices). RULES. (a) SENTENCES: emit one statement per sentence. If a paragraph has more than one sentence, give each its own statement with ids suffixed .s1, .s2, and so on. Abbreviations and legal citations ('U.S.C.', 'CFR', '§', 'et seq.') do not end a sentence. (b) LISTS: when text introduces a list (usually ends with a colon, for example 'The USDA CIO will:'), emit the introducing text as one statement with statement_kind 'lead_in', and emit EVERY item of the list as its own statement with statement_kind 'list_item' and parent_statement_id set to the id of the lead_in. Never skip list items, including lists of legal authorities. For a list inside a list, parent_statement_id is the immediate parent. (c) NEVER merge text from different sentences, paragraphs, or list items into one statement. (d) Copy text exactly; do not summarize. (e) PRONOUNS: when a sentence's subject is a pronoun ('It', 'Its', 'They') that refers to a named actor in the preceding sentence, resolve it: set actor_name to that actor and actor_basis to resolved_from_prior_sentence. (f) DOCUMENT AS SUBJECT: when the grammatical subject is the document itself ('This DR', 'This policy', 'Nothing in this DR'), leave actor_name out; the entities the document acts on belong in target.

statement_id.description: Printed numbering path of the statement: section number, then paragraph letter, then item number in parentheses, for example '1', '3.a', '5.d.s2', '6.a(1)'. Add '.sN' only when a paragraph contains more than one sentence. Must be unique within the document.

statement_kind.description: standalone: a complete sentence that stands on its own. lead_in: text that introduces a list and is incomplete without its items. list_item: a list item that completes its lead_in.

parent_statement_id.description: Include ONLY when statement_kind is list_item: the statement_id of its immediate lead_in. For every other statement leave this field out entirely; never return an empty string.

section_number.description: Number of the section containing the statement, digits only, for example '6'.

section_title.description: Title of the section containing the statement, as shown in the table of contents, for example 'Roles and Responsibilities'.

source_text.description: VERBATIM text of this one sentence or list item exactly as printed, including trailing punctuation such as ':' or ';' and including any list-ending words such as 'and'. No paraphrase, no ellipses, no text from any other statement. For a list_item, give only the item's own text, not the lead_in.

statement_function.description: What the statement does. obligation: a required action or compliance requirement on an actor. responsibility: a standing duty or function assigned to an actor, including present-tense descriptions of what a body does. role_designation: assigns an entity to a role, for example membership or voting status. authority: names a legal source of authority or a grant of authority. scope: states what or whom the document applies to. purpose: states why the document or a body exists. definition: defines a term. condition: states a standalone triggering condition. exception: carves out an exception. savings_clause: states that the document does not displace existing authorities or delegations. effectivity: states when the document takes effect or how long it lasts. supersession: states that the document replaces another. classification_rule: states a rule that classifies something or applies a requirement when a status is met. reference: points to another document or location. inquiry: tells who may be contacted. container: use for every lead_in statement. other: none of the above.

modal_verb.description: The modal word or phrase of the statement's MAIN clause, exactly as written, for example 'will', 'can', 'may', 'must', 'shall', 'must not'. Ignore modals inside relative or subordinate clauses (for 'advises the USDA CIO on IT matters that may become IT investments', the 'may' is not the statement's modal). For a list_item whose own text has no modal, copy the modal from its lead_in. Leave out if the main clause has no modal.

modal_use.description: deontic: the main-clause modal directs, permits, or prohibits action by an actor (for example 'The Deputy CIO will serve', 'can direct questions'). predictive: the modal only states what will happen or remain true (for example 'It will remain in effect until superseded'). none: the main clause has no modal.

normative_force.description: mandatory: deontic 'will', 'shall', or 'must' directing an actor to act or to serve in a role. prohibitive: deontic 'must not', 'shall not', or 'may not'. permissive: deontic 'may' or 'can'. assigned: a present-tense statement with no deontic modal that assigns or describes a function, duty, or role of a named actor (for example 'The CIO Council advises the USDA CIO on...', 'It assesses the needs of...'); use it only when actor_name is present, and never for purpose statements. descriptive: everything else with no deontic force, including purpose, scope, supersession, effectivity, savings clauses, references, authorities, definitions, and statements about the document itself or about other documents. not_applicable: use for every lead_in; its force is carried by its list_items.

actor_name.description: The entity directed to act, permitted to act, or assigned a function or role by this statement, spelled exactly as in the matching actors[].name. It must appear in source_text or in the lead_in's text (leading article removed); for a resolved pronoun, copy it from the antecedent sentence. Leave out when the statement binds no actor: scope, supersession, effectivity, savings clauses, statements about documents (including bylaws), and any statement whose subject is the document itself ('This DR', 'This policy', 'Nothing in this DR'). Never supply an actor that is not stated in the text or resolvable from the preceding sentence. Always leave out for lead_in statements.

actor_basis.description: Include ONLY when actor_name is present; otherwise leave this field out entirely. explicit_in_statement: the actor appears in this statement's own source_text. inherited_from_lead_in: the actor appears only in the lead_in that this list_item completes. resolved_from_prior_sentence: the subject is a pronoun resolved to the actor named in the preceding sentence.

target.description: VERBATIM phrase naming what the action is directed at or what the statement applies to, starting at the first word after any leading article ('a', 'an', 'the'). For a role_designation, the body or unit the role is within (for example 'CIO Council'). Leave out if none.

resulting_status.description: VERBATIM phrase naming the status or role that a role_designation or classification_rule confers, for example 'voting member' or 'advisory (non-voting) members'. Leave out for other statements.

conditions.description: VERBATIM phrases that restrict when or to what the statement applies, for example 'that the CIO Council designates as enterprise initiatives'. Do NOT treat a non-restrictive descriptive phrase set off by commas (for example 'appointed by the USDA CIO' in 'The Secretariat, appointed by the USDA CIO, will serve') as a condition. Leave out if there are none.

items.description: One verbatim condition phrase copied from source_text.

cross_references.description: Other documents, laws, or regulations cited in source_text, each copied verbatim as ONE entry per cited authority, including its code citation (for example 'The Clinger-Cohen Act of 1996, 40 United States Code (U.S.C.) § 11101 et seq.' is one entry; for a list_item that is just a citation, the entry is the item text without the trailing ';' or 'and'). Never add a separate entry for a title that is part of the same citation (the words 'Chief Information Officer' after '7 CFR § 2.32'). Never list generic categories such as 'law' or 'Federal regulation'. Leave out if none.

acronyms.description: Acronyms and abbreviations listed in the acronym appendix, one entry per row, in order. Return an empty list if the document has no acronym appendix.

acronym.description: Acronym or abbreviation exactly as printed.

authorities_and_references.description: Entries of the Authorities and References appendix, one per entry, each copied verbatim, including any date, in order. Return an empty list if the document has no such appendix.

items.description: One appendix entry exactly as printed, joined across line breaks.

policy_statements.source_text: This regulation provides policies and guidelines for the design and publication of Department of Agriculture (USDA) organizational and personal Web pages.
policy_statements.target: design and publication of Department of Agriculture (USDA) organizational and personal Web pages

policy_statements.source_text: These Web pages, including Web-based application pages, are accessible by members of the public who have access to the Internet for telecommunications connectivity and use World Wide Web software browsers for search and retrieval services.
policy_statements.target: members of the public who have access to the Internet for telecommunications connectivity and use World Wide Web software browsers for search and retrieval services

policy_statements.source_text: A Web site provides the public with an introduction to or “picture” of an organizational unit.

The Web site may describe the unit’s mission and major programs; provide guidance on ways to access significant contacts or data and information; and offer hyperlinks to other organizational units, including subordinate units, and/or to organizations outside the unit.

This regulation is designed to ensure a standard, consistent, “look and feel” for all USDA Web sites and Web-based applications, while encouraging innovation in the current fast-moving software technology environment and minimizing constraints on ways in which agencies present material to the public.
policy_statements.target: all USDA Web sites and Web-based applications

policy_statements.source_text: This document is intended to express basic policies and guidelines rather than to serve as a “how to” manual on Web page design.
This regulation supersedes DR-3430-001, dated December 24, 2003.

Electronic information technologies such as the World Wide Web can be used to provide access to information that is well organized, easily found and retrieved, and offered at reasonable cost to information users and providers alike.
These technologies provide a very effective way to communicate with members of the public who have access to the Internet through the use of personal or publicly available microcomputers.

An additional advantage of using the World Wide Web is that it offers multimedia capabilities, including sound (e.g., music and voice) and images (e.g., pictures, maps, and graphics) that can greatly increase the effectiveness of a Web page.
The power and utility of the World Wide Web is related to its ability to provide hyperlinks to associated documents.
Such hyperlinks allow the user to easily access other sites, other documents, and other sections of the same document.
Typically, hyperlinks are activated simply by selecting or “clicking on” a portion of text or an image that has been rendered as a hyperlink.
Linked text is referred to as hypertext.

To achieve the desired benefits of a successful public Internet-based information service and to avoid the frustrations of an unsuccessful one, the following considerations should be kept in mind in planning and designing such a service:
Web sites should be accessible to users with limited as well as full access capabilities.
policy_statements.target: users with limited as well as full access capabilities

policy_statements.source_text: Web page designers should be aware that many users’ available microcomputer and telecommunications technologies may lack the speed and capacity of those available to the designers.
policy_statements.target: many users’ available microcomputer and telecommunications technologies

policy_statements.source_text: Many users still access the Internet through a standard dial-up connection and have a narrow bandwidth communications capability.
Some users, especially users dependent on screen reading software, will have text-only capabilities.
Information should be appropriate and presented in an organized manner.
One major advantage of the World Wide Web is that it allows users to move easily from one linked site to another, thus accessing the Web sites of other organizations worldwide.
If a linkage system is not properly designed, however, users can easily get “lost” and not recognize the significance or even the originator of the information they have accessed.
An organized design incorporating the totality of information available about USDA is critical to the presentation of an accurate picture of the Department.
Typically, many people are involved in generating information from a variety of sources to post on Departmental and agency Web sites.

These content providers, the designated Web site manager (also referred to as a “webmaster” or the assigned system administrator) must cooperatively act with these individuals to ensure that the Web sites and associated documents present an accurate, descriptive, and representative image of the entire Department or agency and its work rather than an image that is fragmented, misleading, or incomplete.
policy_statements.actor_name: These content providers, the designated Web site manager

policy_statements.source_text: The reality of worldwide access should be recognized.
Web sites must be designed with the realization that the public documents they contain are accessible through an international network to users worldwide.
User anonymity must be maintained.
Web servers referenced in this regulation provide open service to the public and must accept outside users without requiring either a local user account or a password.
policy_statements.actor_name: Web servers referenced in this regulation

policy_statements.source_text: USDA fully supports the establishment of any open information server and service that
supports authorized mission-related activities of USDA,
is consistent with prudent operational and security considerations,
provides the public with easy electronic access to information about or disseminated by their Government, and
addresses the accessibility needs of individuals with disabilities as described in Section 508 of the Rehabilitation Act.

Federal agencies and employees are encouraged to maintain open electronic communication with the public while recognizing that with this privilege comes the responsibility to use the electronic forum wisely in serving the public interest.
To facilitate communication between users and USDA, an e-mail contact shall be listed on the home page.
Only public information approved for public release through standard USDA review and clearance processes will be maintained on Web sites or made accessible through links to other Web pages.
policy_statements.target: public information approved for public release through standard USDA review and clearance processes

policy_statements.source_text: Unless an exception has been approved, links shall be made only to Government web pages.
conditions: Unless an exception has been approved

policy_statements.source_text: Exceptions must be approved in advance by the USDA Office of Communications.
Each home page must include a link to the “USDA Quality of Information Guidelines” as well as to agency-specific information on whom to contact to seek correction of USDA-disseminated information.
policy_statements.target: link to the “USDA Quality of Information Guidelines”

policy_statements.source_text: Security is a major consideration in the implementation of any open public access system.
The planned approach to creation of a Web site must include attention to Web site security, including firewalls and other isolation techniques.
policy_statements.target: Web site security, including firewalls and other isolation techniques

policy_statements.source_text: Agency security officers must be consulted as to the technical operation of Web sites.
(See additional security references in Section 5.)

Personal Web pages are permitted for individual employees in their official capacities if the information provided on the pages relates to and supports authorized USDA missions, such as descriptions of a USDA scientist’s research, rather than serving to aggrandize any individual.
conditions: if the information provided on the pages relates to and supports authorized USDA missions, such as descriptions of a USDA scientist’s research, rather than serving to aggrandize any individual

policy_statements.source_text: USDA employees establishing personal Web pages on official Web sites that are accessible by the public must follow the guidelines outlined in this regulation.
policy_statements.actor_name: USDA employees establishing personal Web pages on official Web sites that are accessible by the public

policy_statements.source_text: USDA and agency/staff office home pages shall be linked with the USDA Privacy Policy statement.
policy_statements.actor_name: USDA and agency/staff office home pages

policy_statements.source_text: Any agency with unique privacy requirements, other than or in addition to those outlined in the USDA Privacy Policy statement, may establish and provide a hyperlink to its own privacy statement page.
policy_statements.actor_name: Any agency with unique privacy requirements
conditions: with unique privacy requirements, other than or in addition to those outlined in the USDA Privacy Policy statement

policy_statements.source_text: Agency privacy policy statements are subject to clearance requirements and must be linked with the USDA Privacy Policy statement.
Persistent cookies should not be used on USDA Web sites, or by contractors in designing and/or managing Web sites on behalf of USDA agencies, unless all the following conditions are met:
conditions: unless all the following conditions are met

policy_statements.source_text: A compelling need to gather the data on the site exists, and a cookie provides the best means of obtaining the data.
Appropriate and publicly disclosed privacy safeguards are in place for the handling of information derived from the cookie.
Clear, conspicuous notice is provided on the Web site that a cookie is being used.
The Secretary of Agriculture has approved use of the cookie.

In addition, all USDA Web sites, including sites designed, operated, or managed by contractors on behalf of USDA agencies, shall comply with the standards set forth in the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act of 1998 with respect to the collection of personal information online at Web sites directed to children.
cross_references: Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act of 1998
policy_statements.target: standards set forth in the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act of 1998

policy_statements.source_text: All information under consideration for publication in Web sites must be evaluated to determine whether the information constitutes Sensitive Security Information (SSI).
policy_statements.target: All information under consideration for publication in Web sites

policy_statements.source_text: SSI may not be made available except as described by USDA Departmental Regulation 3440-002, “Control and Protection of ‘Sensitive Security Information.’”
cross_references: USDA Departmental Regulation 3440-002, “Control and Protection of ‘Sensitive Security Information.’”
conditions: except as described by USDA Departmental Regulation 3440-002, “Control and Protection of ‘Sensitive Security Information.’”

policy_statements.source_text: All USDA Internet Web sites must comply with provisions stated in the USDA Web Style Guide.
policy_statements.target: provisions stated in the USDA Web Style Guide

policy_statements.source_text: The Guide defines guidelines and standards for look, feel, and navigation to promote consistency while also improving the overall user experience.

Guide provisions apply to Web-based application pages which can be viewed by external customers, and include any Web page or application that target all USDA employees, such as a USDA enterprise application.
policy_statements.target: Web-based application pages which can be viewed by external customers

policy_statements.source_text: Agency IntrAnet sites or other internal Web sites or Web applications, which are inaccessible to the public and used for internal nonpublic purposes, may not be required to use the guidance presented in the USDA Web Style Guide depending on the organization’s mission
policy_statements.target: guidance presented in the USDA Web Style Guide
conditions: which are inaccessible to the public and used for internal nonpublic purposes

policy_statements.source_text: Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act of 1998.
cross_references: Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act of 1998

policy_statements.source_text: Computer Security Act of 1987.
USDA Departmental Regulation 3140-1, “USDA Information Systems Security Policy.”
cross_references: USDA Departmental Regulation 3140-1, “USDA Information Systems Security Policy.”

policy_statements.source_text: USDA Departmental Regulation 3140-2, “USDA Internet Security Policy.”
cross_references: USDA Departmental Regulation 3140-2, “USDA Internet Security Policy.”

cross_references: USDA Departmental Regulation 3300-1, “USDA Telecommunications and Internet Services and Use.”

USDA Departmental Regulation 3440-002, “Control and Protection of ‘Sensitive Security Information.’”
cross_references: USDA Departmental Regulation 3440-002, “Control and Protection of ‘Sensitive Security Information.’”

cross_references: USDA Departmental Regulation 4030-001, “Section 508 Implementation Final Guidance.”

policy_statements.source_text: The Privacy Act of 1974.
USDA Privacy Policy.
USDA Web Style Guide.
Browser. A shortened term for Web Browser.
A browser is software used on the World Wide Web to access and/or retrieve documents through the use of Internet addresses known as “URLs.”
Locating documents on the World Wide Web is facilitated through the use of hyperlinks in hypertext documents.
Browsers may support only line mode, full-screen, or graphics including pictures and sound.
Many browsers with various capabilities and platforms are available.
Some browsers are proprietary and must be purchased, whereas others are available at no cost by downloading from a server.
Examples of currently available browsers that should be supported include Internet Explorer, Netscape Navigator, Mozilla, Opera, and Safari.
Dead link. A link to a nonexistent or non-operational page or server.
Firewall. A dedicated device (hardware and software) placed between internal and external networks to control access and prevent misuse and abuse
Home page. Primary page or starting point, often reached through a uniform resource locator (URL).
Although a home page is described as a single document, it can contain multiple screens.
An organizational home page contains information about a definable organization such as USDA, an agency, or a division of an agency.
A personal Web page contains information related to an individual employee (e.g., a scientist whose work may be of interest to the public).
See Section 4.e.
HTML. HyperText Markup Language.
HTML is the standard language used to produce Web pages and hyperlinks to other documents.

Because this is a rapidly evolving technology, and because adherence to the international standards is voluntary, some variation exists in the versions of HTML available and the HTML features supported by various browsers.
Agencies and offices need to be aware of these differences in electing a version to use.
USDA will not adopt any single version of HTML.
ISSPM. Information Systems Security Program Manager.

Public document. Any document or information not subject to access limitations due to national security classification, the Privacy Act, Freedom of Information Act exemptions, or copyright protection.
Secondary pages. Additional pages, linked to a home page, or to another secondary page, containing additional information or resources.
SSI. Sensitive Security Information.
Unclassified information of a sensitive nature, further defined in Departmental Regulation 3440-002, “Control and Protection of ‘Sensitive Security Information.’”
cross_references: Departmental Regulation 3440-002, “Control and Protection of ‘Sensitive Security Information.’”

policy_statements.source_text: URL. Uniform Resource Locator.
A URL is the address of a resource such as a home page.
The address syntax also defines the type of resource, as follows: scheme://host.domain[:port]/path/filename.
The USDA home page URL, for example, is  http://www.usda.gov
Web page. A document designed for access using a browser and developed in accordance with the HTML Web format standard.
Typically, such documents are posted on an Internet or Intranet site.

World Wide Web (or WWW; also referred to as “the Web”). A hypertext-based client/server application that guides the user to a linked collection of information in a hypertext markup language available through the Internet and accessible through common browsing software.
Design approach
USDA Internet Web sites must comply with the USDA Web Style Guide .
A Web site or Web-based application shall be linked with metadata that describes information and data available to the public upon request.
policy_statements.target: metadata that describes information and data available to the public upon request

policy_statements.source_text: The Web site shall be structured around the mission of the organization and the information the organization wishes to convey to the public.

The information and data an agency or office plans to present must be organized and its Web pages structured to provide the user with the efficient presentation and navigation of the organization’s information.
A “tree” structure can be useful for organizing information, though given the versatility of hypertext linkages, other modes of organization can also be effective.
An organization’s home page should be limited to a description of the organization’s mission, functions, employees, and information resources.
It would be inappropriate, for example, for a division’s home page to describe the mission or functions of the entire agency.
Designers are encouraged to review the Web sites of other organizations on the Internet to become familiar with designs that are effective.
policy_statements.target: Web sites of other organizations on the Internet

policy_statements.source_text: Agency program and public affairs staffs will develop each Web site jointly.
policy_statements.actor_name: Agency program and public affairs staffs

policy_statements.source_text: The appropriate agency Information Systems Security Program Manager should be consulted regarding technical security issues prior to posting online.
policy_statements.actor_name: appropriate agency Information Systems Security Program Manager

policy_statements.source_text: Web pages shall be designed to support users (e.g., with limited access capabilities such as text-only browsers) who cannot or who do not wish to access pictures, graphics, or sound as well as to support users with full access capabilities.
A Web page under development should be reviewed and tested thoroughly—preferably by an independent tester using a wide variety of browsers—before release to the public.
If particular versions of browsers are required to access the content, those limitations should be explicit on the page or on a technical page accessible through the Web page.
conditions: If particular versions of browsers are required to access the content

policy_statements.source_text: Content
Web pages should be kept simple to avoid a cluttered or confusing appearance.
As a general “rule of thumb,” a list or menu should be limited to ten or less items, and a maximum of 15.
Only USDA symbols approved by the Office of Communications or a duly authorized agency representative should be used.
Agencies that are undergoing reorganization and do not have an appropriate logo should use the USDA symbol.
policy_statements.actor_name: Agencies that are undergoing reorganization and do not have an appropriate logo
conditions: that are undergoing reorganization and do not have an appropriate logo

policy_statements.source_text: Secondary pages should contain navigational aids to assist the user in returning to previous pages or directly to the home page of the organization.
Links to governmental material outside USDA shall be identified clearly.
(See Section 7. c. 2 & 3 for additional requirements regarding linking to nongovernmental or private sector Websites).
Links to proprietary information or formats should be annotated appropriately.
Links to large documents should inform about the file size of the document and warn of anticipated downloading time, if the time is lengthy.
Each Web page shall capture the most recent update of page information as part of the page metadata.
policy_statements.target: most recent update of page information

policy_statements.source_text: Agencies and staff offices may display the date of the most recent update within the content area of the Web page.
policy_statements.target: date of the most recent update

policy_statements.source_text: Each Web site should invite users to submit comments or suggestions about page content via hyperlinks to user evaluation forms or by other means, such as an online e-mail form addressed to the Webmaster or to Contact Us.
The use of “dead” hyperlinks is not permitted.

extract_result.purpose:
This regulation provides policies and guidelines for the design and publication of Department of Agriculture (USDA) organizational and personal Web pages. These Web pages, including Web-based application pages, are accessible by members of the public who have access to the Internet for telecommunications connectivity and use World Wide Web software browsers for search and retrieval services.
A Web site provides the public with an introduction to or “picture” of an organizational unit. The Web site may describe the unit’s mission and major programs; provide guidance on ways to access significant contacts or data and information; and offer hyperlinks to other organizational units, including subordinate units, and/or to organizations outside the unit.
This regulation is designed to ensure a standard, consistent, “look and feel” for all USDA Web sites and Web-based applications, while encouraging innovation in the current fast-moving software technology environment and minimizing constraints on ways in which agencies present material to the public. This document is intended to express basic policies and guidelines rather than to serve as a “how to” manual on Web page design.

This regulation supersedes DR-3430-001, dated December 24, 2003.

Electronic information technologies such as the World Wide Web can be used to provide access to information that is well organized, easily found and retrieved, and offered at reasonable cost to information users and providers alike.
These technologies provide a very effective way to communicate with members of the public who have access to the Internet through the use of personal or publicly available microcomputers.

An additional advantage of using the World Wide Web is that it offers multimedia capabilities, including sound (e.g., music and voice) and images (e.g., pictures, maps, and graphics) that can greatly increase the effectiveness of a Web page.
The power and utility of the World Wide Web is related to its ability to provide hyperlinks to associated documents.
Such hyperlinks allow the user to easily access other sites, other documents, and other sections of the same document.
Typically, hyperlinks are activated simply by selecting or “clicking on” a portion of text or an image that has been rendered as a hyperlink.
Linked text is referred to as hypertext.

To achieve the desired benefits of a successful public Internet-based information service and to avoid the frustrations of an unsuccessful one, the following considerations should be kept in mind in planning and designing such a service:
Web sites should be accessible to users with limited as well as full access capabilities.
users with limited as well as full access capabilities
Web page designers should be aware that many users’ available microcomputer and telecommunications technologies may lack the speed and capacity of those available to the designers.
many users’ available microcomputer and telecommunications technologies
Many users still access the Internet through a standard dial-up connection and have a narrow bandwidth communications capability.
Some users, especially users dependent on screen reading software, will have text-only capabilities.
Information should be appropriate and presented in an organized manner.
One major advantage of the World Wide Web is that it allows users to move easily from one linked site to another, thus accessing the Web sites of other organizations worldwide.
If a linkage system is not properly designed, however, users can easily get “lost” and not recognize the significance or even the originator of the information they have accessed.
An organized design incorporating the totality of information available about USDA is critical to the presentation of an accurate picture of the Department.
Typically, many people are involved in generating information from a variety of sources to post on Departmental and agency Web sites.
These content providers, the designated Web site manager
The reality of worldwide access should be recognized.
Web sites must be designed with the realization that the public documents they contain are accessible through an international network to users worldwide.

Browser.** A shortened term for Web Browser
A browser is software used on the World Wide Web to access and/or retrieve documents through the use of Internet addresses known as “URLs.”
Locating documents on the World Wide Web is facilitated through the use of hyperlinks in hypertext documents.
Browsers may support only line mode, full-screen, or graphics including pictures and sound.
Many browsers with various capabilities and platforms are available.
Some browsers are proprietary and must be purchased, whereas others are available at no cost by downloading from a server.
Examples of currently available browsers that should be supported include Internet Explorer, Netscape Navigator, Mozilla, Opera, and Safari.
Dead link.** A link to a nonexistent or non-operational page or server
c **Firewall.** A dedicated device (hardware and software) placed between internal and external networks to control access and prevent misuse and abuse
d **Home page.** Primary page or starting point, often reached through a uniform resource locator (URL
Although a home page is described as a single document, it can contain multiple screens.
An organizational home page contains information about a definable organization such as USDA, an agency, or a division of an agency.
A personal Web page contains information related to an individual employee (e.g., a scientist whose work may be of interest to the public).
HTML is the standard language used to produce Web pages and hyperlinks to other documents.

Because this is a rapidly evolving technology, and because adherence to the international standards is voluntary, some variation exists in the versions of HTML available and the HTML features supported by various browsers.
Agencies and offices need to be aware of these differences in electing a version to use.
USDA will not adopt any single version of HTML.
